# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–30 (Complete – Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of eighth year after Waterloo, continuing into summer and now winter. Year is 1830 (French Revolution year).
- **Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens," near Queen's Crawley); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall (Carbury Manor House); Carbury Chase; Beccles; Quenwick; Harrowgate.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley**: Died peacefully; buried at Brompton.
- **Mr. Osborne**: Deceased (four days after stroke); Major Dobbin appointed executor; Georgy established as heir.
- **Joseph Sedley**: Died at Aix-la-Chapelle three months after Dobbin's final visit. Heavily insured (£2,000); legacy split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (appointed administratrix). All other property in valueless shares.
- **Colonel Rawdon Crawley**: Died of yellow fever at Coventry Island; estate devolved upon Sir Pitt's son, now Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.
- **Sir Pitt**: Died six weeks after Colonel Rawdon.

## Rebecca's Arc (Chapters 27–30)
**Seduction and Enslavement of Jos Sedley**: At Pumpernickel, Rebecca (Madame de Raudon, formerly with Rawdon Crawley) seduced Jos through calculated performance—hiding degradation evidence, offering tender looks, falsely claiming virtuous past. Led him to Room No. 92, Elephant lodging-house. Within week, Jos became her "entirely slave." Changed habits; praised Dobbin constantly to Emmy; told her she behaved cruelly toward him. Lived in Brussels hotel in genteel manner with adjacent suite, carriage, entertainments.

**Dobbin's Opposition and Departure**: Called her "the little minx"; stormed at Jos. Amelia embraced Becky warmly and flung Dobbin an angry, scornful glance—the most unjust of her life. **Dobbin had spent fifteen years devoted to Amelia; she grew accustomed to trampling on him but did not wish to marry him—only to keep him.** Dobbin departed with haughty bow.

**Insurance and Death**: Jos effected heavy insurance; Dobbin procured prolonged leave, went alarmed. Jos died three months later at Aix-la-Chapelle. Insurance company challenged payment; Rebecca dared them to refuse, declared herself victim of "infamous conspiracy." Solicitors Messrs. Burke, Thurtell, and Hayes triumphed; £2,000 paid, split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (administratrix). **Dobbin sent back his share and rigidly declined communication with Rebecca.**

**Final State**: Never became Lady Crawley though styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) declined to see her; receives liberal allowance. Appears very wealthy. Chiefly at Bath and Cheltenham, where strong party considers her "most injured woman." Busies herself in works of piety, church attendance with footman, appears on all Charity Lists, has stalls at Fancy Fairs.

## Amelia and William Dobbin's Resolution (Chapter 29)
**Becky's Revelation**: At Ostend, Becky revealed George Osborne was "selfish humbug, low-bred cockney dandy...who had neither wit, nor manners, nor heart." Produced letter: George "wanted me to run away with him—gave it me under your nose, the day before he was shot." **"Dobbin forced him to keep his word."**

**Amelia's Transformation**: Emmy wept; internal struggle: "Was she most grieved because the idol of her life was tumbled down...or glad because the barrier was removed which modesty had placed between her and a new, a real affection? 'There is nothing to forbid me now,' she thought. 'I may love him with all my heart now.'"

**Marriage and Life**: Two mornings later at Dike, Amelia went to Dobbin "in dripping white bonnet and shawl...kissing one of his hands with all her might." Only Georgy and Jos present at ceremony. Emmy told William: "Never speak of that day again." Dobbin quit service immediately, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane (christened by Rev. James Crawley) than of his History of the Punjaub. Lady Jane godmother to Mrs. Dobbin's child; they became great friends.

## Supporting Characters—Old
- **Glorvina O'Dowd**: Married Major Posky after his first wife's death. Colonel Sir Michael O'Dowd advanced to Major-General; Lady O'Dowd lives in "great splendour at O'Dowdstown."
- **George Osborne (son)**: "Dashing young gentleman"; hunted and shot with Rawdon; at Cambridge; quarrelled with Rawdon over Lady Jane's daughter.
- **Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.** (young baronet): Lives at Queen's Crawley with Lady Jane and daughter; declined to see mother Rebecca.

## Lady Carbury and Family (Chapter 30)
**Character**: Lives modestly on Welbeck Street with son Felix and daughter Henrietta. **"The woman was false from head to foot, but there was much of good in her, false though she was."** Devoted to children, especially Felix. No ambition to write good books; painfully anxious to write ones critics would praise through inducing their commendation.

**Workspace**: Back drawing-room (divided by permanently closed doors) is workspace for writing books and contriving systems to inveigle editors and critics.

**Felix Carbury** (son): Beautiful as a star; cynosure of mother's eyes. Mother spoilt him as boy and man; almost proud of his vices. Philosophy: "carpe diem." Possesses two unpaid-for horses. Demands money from mother to maintain appearance in Grosvenor Square. Recently won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough and £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. **Currently considering courtship of Marie Melmotte (great heiress); at Melmotte ball, waltzes with Marie and studies words as lesson ("I do"), repeating them to convince poor girl he could love her.** Left ball early to Beargarden—gambling devil hot within him.

**Henrietta Carbury** (daughter): Romance commenced. Cousin Roger Carbury (of Carbury Hall, nearly forty) passionately in love with her. Paul Montague is another gentleman whom Henrietta has seen.

**Felix's Financial Crisis**: Since Roger's offer, Felix has "gone on from bad to worse, till his condition had become one of hopeless embarrassment." Lady Carbury constantly appeals to Roger Carbury for advice—which she never follows. Roger recommended she give up house in town, find home for daughter elsewhere, and let Felix "bear the brunt of his own misdoings." Roger spoke severely of Felix; recently came to London, closeted with Lady Carbury in back drawing-room to address "the indispensable necessity...of taking some steps by which at any rate the young man's present expenses might be brought to an end." Roger horrified that man with no income has hunters.

**Roger's Concerns**: Lady Carbury mentioned notes and gold on Felix's table—"ever so much"—suggesting recent gambling winnings. Roger declared: "I can understand that you should provide him with bed and food, but not that you should pander to his vices by giving him money." Lady Carbury hopes if Felix won money, he would let her have some, as she "hardly know[s] how to turn."

## The Melmottes (Chapter 30)
**Augustus Melmotte, Esq.**: Arrived in London from Paris within last two years; previously M. Melmotte. Claims English birth though speaks native language fluently with accent betraying "long expatriation." In City, his name "worth any money,--though his character was perhaps worth but little."

**Madame Melmotte**: Said to have been Bohemian Jewess; admits to being foreigner, speaks very little English. Birthplace of daughter disputed: some say New York; Madame declares Paris.

**Marie Melmotte**: Spoke as Mademoiselle Marie; now speaks English well as foreigner. **Has begun forming own opinions; absolutely rejected Lord Grasslough** (bankrupt, no income, ugly, vicious, ill-tempered). Had experience with Lord Nidderdale, who half-laughingly said he "might just as well take her for his wife." Now contemplating own happiness. **People saying if Sir Felix Carbury managed affairs well he might be the happy man.**

**Melmotte Wealth**: As affairs prospered, immediate disposition of Marie became less necessary; Melmotte reduced offers for suitors. Visible wealth certain: house, furniture, carriages, horses, servants with livery and powdered heads, gems, presents. Two dinner parties daily. Tradesmen "quite free of doubt"; "money in daily use" evident.

## Roger Carbury of Carbury Hall (Chapter 30)
**Character and Standing**: Never owed shilling he could not pay; father before him likewise. Orders to Beccles tradesmen not extensive; care taken goods neither overcharged nor unnecessary. Tradesmen consequently did not care much for him, though elders entertained ancient reverence for family. "Carbury of Carbury"—distinction of itself. Carbury parish named for family. Carbury Chase (partly in Carbury parish, partly Bundlesham) belongs unfortunately in entirety to Bundlesham estate.

## Paul Montague's Love Triangle (Chapter 30, Excerpts 1674–1679)
**First Visit Crisis**: During second visit of Lady Carbury and Henrietta to Carbury Hall, young man Paul Montague (of whom Roger had spoken much) arrived. Roger had anticipated no evil in timing visit; but Paul fell into love with his cousin's guest Henrietta, and "great harm had come of it."

**Roger's Proposal and Offer**: Roger offered hand in marriage to cousin Henrietta with declaration: "Very serious to me. I may say so serious that nothing in my own life can approach it in importance." Made clear resolve to hold to what he believed to be his own, and to fight if fighting necessary.

**Paul's Departure**: Scene between men lasted above an hour. Very hot words exchanged. Paul Montague packed all clothes and was driven away to railway station by Roger himself, without seeing either lady. Last words Roger spoke at platform were not quarrelsome: "God bless you, old fellow," pressing Paul's hands. Paul's eyes full of tears; replied by returning pressure.

**Henrietta's Response**: Not a word said to Lady Carbury or daughter of real cause of Paul's sudden disappearance—attributed to necessary business in London. Before they left Manor, squire pleaded cause with Henrietta in vain. Henrietta colder than ever; said she was "too young to think of marrying yet," implying difference in ages too great. Roger easily countered she would be older in twelvemonth; impossible to convince her any twelvemonths would alter disparity. **But even that disparity was not now her strongest reason for feeling sure that she could not marry Roger Carbury.**

**Paul's Return and Argument**: Within week of Lady Carbury's departure, Paul Montague returned, "and returned as a still dear friend." Had promised before leaving he would not see Henrietta again for three months, "but he would promise nothing further." Argued to Roger: "If she won't take you, there is no reason why I shouldn't try." Roger would not accede to justice of this; believed Paul bound to retire altogether partly from lack of income, partly from Roger's prior claim, partly from gratitude.

**Paul's Justification**: Paul saw Roger's point yet had scruples. Questioned why friend should be "a dog in the manger." Believed he could yield at once to Roger's older claims if Roger could make anything of them. Indeed he could have no chance if girl disposed to take Roger. Roger had advantage of Carbury Manor; Paul had only share in "doubtful business of Fisker, Montague, and Montague, in a wretched little town 250 miles further off than San Francisco!" But if Roger, with all advantages, could not prevail, why should not Paul try? Declared to himself he had money (though doubtful) and would not give up Henrietta on account of finances.

## Lady Carbury's Divided Concerns (Chapter 30, Excerpts 1679–1681)
**Felix's Deterioration and Marriage Strategy**: Lady Carbury's desire for union between Roger and daughter greatly increased by solicitude regarding son. Since Roger's offer, "Felix had gone on from bad to worse, till his condition had become one of hopeless embarrassment." If daughter could be settled in world, Lady Carbury said to herself, she could then devote herself to son's interests. But she paid so much money for him, and would have so much more extracted, that it might come to pass she would be unable to keep home for daughter.

**Additional Details on Coldcombe**: Ridette packed single trunk and moved from Quenwick to Coldcombe. Jotho Corrett followed her to Coldcombe within the month.
